architectural_implications.after: Reasoning block sealed with session/user/prompt-bound AEAD plus HMAC, with stateless verification at re-entry.
architectural_implications.before: Reasoning block encrypted, returned to client as an opaque envelope, accepted back with no binding to session, user, or prompt.
architectural_implications.consequence: Replay and cross-session extraction attacks are blocked, but the API now requires a well-defined context-binding contract and a decision about which context dimensions are carried in the envelope versus held server-side.
architectural_implications.observation: Reasoning envelopes must be authenticated against the context in which they will be replayed rather than merely encrypted.

architectural_implications.after: Replayed reasoning is validated for provenance and context before being admitted, on par with untrusted user text.
architectural_implications.before: Reasoning arriving in a request is treated as previously-generated trusted state and fed directly back into generation.
architectural_implications.consequence: Thought-poisoning and behavioural steering via injected reasoning become detectable; validation logic adds a hop to the request path and requires provenance metadata on every trace.
architectural_implications.observation: Replayed reasoning is an input channel, not a trusted internal channel.

architectural_implications.after: Reasoning withheld, summarized, or returned only as a sealed, context-bound artifact.
architectural_implications.before: Raw chain-of-thought streamed to clients for transparency and visible-thinking UX.
architectural_implications.consequence: Reduces PII/credential leakage and distillation risk while degrading debuggability and user-visible rationale; internal monitoring must then happen server-side, which reintroduces the exposure problem the design was avoiding.
architectural_implications.observation: Whether to return raw reasoning to clients at all becomes an architectural decision, not a UX toggle.

article_ideas.angle: Take the attacker's view: walk through the sealed-envelope round trip, show why the model is a cooperative oracle, then derive the design rule that opaque client-visible blobs must never be accepted back as trusted input unless bound to the context of their replay.
article_ideas.audience: AI platform engineers, API security architects, and lab infrastructure leads
article_ideas.thesis: Encrypting reasoning blocks and returning them to the client provides no protection because the model itself decrypts and honors replayed envelopes; the failure is a context-binding and access-control failure, not a key-strength failure, so any architecture built on 'encrypt harder' is misdiagnosed.
article_ideas.title: Your Model Is the Decryption Oracle: Why Sealed Chain-of-Thought Is Not a Security Boundary

article_ideas.angle: Frame the tradeoff as an architectural budget problem: enumerate what oversight is lost when reasoning is withheld, what leaks when it is returned, and argue for privileged server-side auditing rather than client-visible traces.
article_ideas.audience: Alignment and evals practitioners, AI governance teams, enterprise risk owners
article_ideas.based_on: The same trace that is a safety-assurance asset is also an exfiltration asset
article_ideas.thesis: Chain-of-thought visibility is simultaneously a safety-assurance asset and an exfiltration asset, so monitorability stacks built on third-party reasoning APIs are structurally fragile and should be designed with the assumption that the surface will be withdrawn or obfuscated.
article_ideas.title: The Observability Surface Is the Attack Surface: Monitoring and Anti-Extraction Cannot Both Win

article_ideas.angle: Evidence-driven: anchors on the corpus scan and the public-repo findings, then gives a concrete classification and retention policy for traces that matches the policy already applied to raw user input.
article_ideas.audience: Data platform and security engineers, compliance leads at enterprises consuming frontier reasoning APIs
article_ideas.based_on: Scratchpads, traces, and intermediate artifacts are effectively unredacted copies of the full input distribution
article_ideas.thesis: Reasoning traces are unredacted serializations of the full input distribution, so treating them as metadata rather than user-content-grade data silently creates credential and PII egress through logs, observability tooling, and public repositories.
article_ideas.title: Your Scratchpad Is Raw User Input: Data Classification for Reasoning Traces

article_ideas.angle: Contrast text-channel injection defenses with the reasoning channel, show why provenance must determine trust rather than artifact type, and specify the admission-control hop agents need on re-entry.
article_ideas.audience: Agent framework authors, LLM application security teams
article_ideas.based_on: trust must follow provenance, not artifact type
article_ideas.thesis: Thought poisoning moves part of the prompt-injection surface out of natural-language instructions and into replayed reasoning, where instruction-hierarchy defenses and input filters do not operate, so agents that persist reasoning across turns inherit a persistent injection vector they cannot currently see.
article_ideas.title: The Reasoning Layer Is the New Injection Layer

connections.relationship: Applies authenticated encryption with associated data to bind a reasoning envelope to its originating session and request context.
Serves as a low-compute distillation channel, letting smaller family models absorb frontier reasoning behaviour from extracted traces.
Extends the injection surface from user-visible text into the replayable reasoning layer, bypassing instruction-hierarchy defenses aimed at text inputs.
Turns traces and logs into an unredacted copy of model input, requiring input-grade data classification for trace storage.

evidence_quotes.text: Models encrypt thinking and return it in a sealed envelope to the client.
Passing encrypted thoughts back to the model via API calls to extract reasoning.
Universal jailbreak decodes the reasoning of Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models.

core_insights.generalization: Whenever a service returns opaque, authenticated-looking blobs to a client and also accepts those blobs back as input, the service's own processing capacity becomes an oracle that defeats the wrapping. This applies to signed state blobs, stateful tool tokens, and delegated capability handles, not just reasoning traces.
core_insights.insight: Encrypted chain-of-thought blocks returned by frontier APIs are not secrets at all — they are portable ciphertext that the model itself will decrypt, making the model the decryption oracle. Because the envelope is not bound to the request context, an attacker can feed the sealed block back through API calls to recover the full reasoning trace; the attack is a universal jailbreak rather than per-prompt exploitation.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It invalidates the assumption that 'encrypted reasoning in a sealed envelope' constitutes a security boundary. Any design that treats client-visible reasoning ciphertext as opaque and untrusted-but-safe is fundamentally broken; the threat model must assume the model will cooperate with an attacker's replay request.

evidence_quotes.text: Smaller LLMs within the same family can decode reasoning traces of frontier models like GPT-4 or Claude Opus.
Extracted reasoning blocks are portable across user sessions and models.
Taking reasoning traces from Opus and injecting them into Kimi or other models.

core_insights.generalization: Any shared-tokenizer or shared-family deployment where a weaker model can consume artifacts produced by a stronger model creates a decoding path; capability gating by model tier is not an information barrier.
core_insights.insight: Reasoning traces are extractable across model boundaries: smaller open-source models within the same family can decode the reasoning blocks of larger frontier models, and extracted blocks are portable across user sessions and across different models. Frontier reasoning is therefore distillable at low marginal compute using a sibling model as the decoder.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Model-family homogeneity becomes an attack surface. Shipping a small sibling model alongside a frontier API (as many labs do) hands attackers the decoder for the frontier model's reasoning, converting reasoning traces into a free distillation channel and collapsing the compute moat reasoning models are meant to provide.

evidence_quotes.text: Poisoned thoughts can be injected into replayed user conversations to induce unintended model behaviors.
Enables advanced prompt injection, model distillation attacks, and behavioral steering at low computational cost.

core_insights.generalization: Any system that treats internally-generated artifacts (plans, scratchpads, memory writes) as trusted when replayed should treat them as untrusted input; trust must follow provenance, not artifact type.
core_insights.insight: Thought poisoning turns replayed reasoning blocks into a control channel: injected or forged reasoning can be replayed inside a user conversation to steer model behaviour. This moves a portion of prompt-injection surface from natural-language instructions into the reasoning layer, where existing input filters and instruction-hierarchy defenses do not operate.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Guardrail stacks generally inspect user-visible text and tool inputs; a poisoned reasoning block arrives in a channel that is presumed trusted and internal. Agents that persist or replay reasoning across turns inherit a persistent, hard-to-audit injection vector.

evidence_quotes.text: Reasoning traces frequently leak PII, technical identifiers, and API keys/credentials.
Dataset scans of 350,000 reasoning blocks revealed hundreds of distinct PII items, technical identifiers, and credentials.

core_insights.generalization: Scratchpads, traces, and intermediate artifacts are effectively unredacted copies of the full input distribution — treat trace storage with the same data-classification and retention rules as raw user input, not as metadata.
core_insights.insight: Reasoning traces are a PII and credential exfiltration surface: scanning 350,000 reasoning blocks surfaced hundreds of distinct PII items, technical identifiers, and credentials, and researchers found hundreds of thousands of reasoning blocks leaked in public GitHub and Hugging Face repositories. Thinking tokens are raw-processing artifacts, so sensitive material passed through the model ends up serialized into the trace.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Any pipeline that logs, stores, or returns reasoning traces inherits the sensitivity of everything the model reasoned over. Enterprises using frontier APIs may be leaking API keys and internal identifiers into logs, observability tooling, and vendor telemetry without an obvious egress point in their data-flow diagram.

evidence_quotes.text: Mitigations include context-based envelope defense, stateless verification, and not returning reasoning to users.
Architectural revisions are required since simple cryptographic wrapping of reasoning blocks is insufficient.
Session-specific AEAD encryption

core_insights.generalization: For any replay-sensitive token (cached tool results, resumable agent state, signed continuations), the design question is which context dimensions — session, user, model, prompt hash — must be authenticated into the token versus held server-side.
core_insights.insight: The proposed mitigation is context binding, not stronger cryptography: reasoning envelopes must be bound to the specific request context using session-specific AEAD, HMAC integrity checks, and stateless verification. Cryptographic wrapping alone is insufficient because the failure is a context-binding and access-control failure, not a key-strength failure.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It reframes reasoning-trace protection from 'encrypt harder' to 'authenticate the binding between artifact and context'. The stateless-verification constraint matters operationally: labs want to verify envelopes without a per-request session store, which pushes the binding into the envelope itself rather than into server-side state.

evidence_quotes.text: How can labs effectively monitor model reasoning without exposing vulnerabilities to extraction attacks?
The illusion of security around proprietary chain-of-thought is broken, necessitating fundamental architectural redesigns.

core_insights.generalization: Observability surfaces frequently double as attack surfaces; a decision to expose an internal artifact for debugging or oversight is simultaneously a decision to widen the leak perimeter.
core_insights.insight: There is an unresolved structural tension between hiding chain-of-thought to protect proprietary reasoning IP against distillation and keeping chain-of-thought visible to enable monitoring, oversight, and reward-hacking detection. The same trace that is a safety-assurance asset is also an exfiltration asset.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Defensive alignment and monitoring pipelines that depend on readable reasoning are in direct conflict with anti-extraction measures. Teams building monitorability on top of third-party reasoning APIs may find that surface withdrawn or obfuscated by the provider for competitive reasons.

project_ideas.name: Provenance-Gated Trace Replay Middleware
project_ideas.poc: Insert middleware between the agent loop's trace persistence layer and model call that requires provenance metadata on every replayed trace and rejects traces lacking context match; run an injection suite where forged reasoning steers behavior, and measure blocked versus passed attacks.

project_ideas.based_on: collapsing the compute moat reasoning models are meant to provide
project_ideas.hypothesis: Capability recovered by a small same-family model from extracted frontier reasoning traces follows a saturating curve in trace fidelity, such that summarization or truncation of traces removes most of the distillation benefit while withholding traces entirely removes only marginally more — meaning hiding chain-of-thought buys less moat than its monitorability cost implies.
project_ideas.measurement: Downstream task accuracy of the small model per fidelity level relative to a no-trace control, and the marginal accuracy delta between summarized and fully withheld traces.
project_ideas.name: Cross-Model Distillation Yield Curve
project_ideas.poc: Take a fixed reasoning-heavy task suite, extract traces at several fidelity levels (full, summarized, truncated, withheld), train or few-shot a small same-family model on each level, and plot capability transfer against fidelity.

project_ideas.based_on: Reasoning traces frequently leak PII, technical identifiers, and API keys/credentials.
project_ideas.hypothesis: A write-time scanner over reasoning traces, logs, and public-repository artifacts detects credential and PII leakage at substantially higher prevalence than equivalent scans over final model outputs, confirming traces are an unredacted copy of the input distribution rather than derived metadata.
project_ideas.measurement: Per-block leakage prevalence in traces versus matched final outputs, distinct credential/PII items found, and debuggability score of redacted versus raw traces.
project_ideas.name: Trace Egress Scanner
project_ideas.poc: Ingest a corpus of reasoning blocks plus matched final outputs, run identical credential/PII detectors over both, and compare hit rates and distinct-entity counts; add a redaction pass and re-measure downstream debuggability of the redacted trace.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Ilia Shumailov & Alexander Panfilov
  • Channel: Machine Learning Street Talk
  • Main topic: Stealing reasoning traces from proprietary LLM APIs via universal jailbreaks and cross-model reasoning extraction
  • Purpose: To analyze and explain the technical details and security implications of extracting, decoding, and repurposing hidden chain-of-thought reasoning traces from frontier large language models. Ilia Shumailov and Alexander Panfilov discuss their research paper, 'Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs', demonstrating how encrypted reasoning blocks (chain-of-thought) from frontier AI models (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google) can be extracted, decrypted, and repurposed using cross-model reasoning extraction attacks. They examine the vulnerabilities in model APIs, safety implications, security mitigation strategies, and the broader debate around AI governance, model theft, and the elusive balance between model monitorability and safety.

Topic Map

Universal Jailbreak and Reasoning Decryption

  • Explanation: Extracting hidden reasoning traces from proprietary frontier AI models by leveraging vulnerabilities in API designs.
  • Key claims:
    • Universal jailbreak decodes the reasoning of Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models.
    • Reasoning token counts match billed API thinking tokens 1:1 for most probed prompts.
    • Models encrypt thinking and return it in a sealed envelope to the client.
  • Examples:
    • Passing encrypted thoughts back to the model via API calls to extract reasoning.
  • Terminology:
    • chain-of-thought
    • encrypted reasoning
    • jailbreak
    • prompt injection
  • Why it matters: Exposes how frontier labs rely on weak API sealing mechanisms to hide internal model reasoning, which can be easily circumvented.

Cross-Model Reasoning Extraction and Thought Poisoning

  • Explanation: Using smaller open-source models within the same family to extract reasoning traces from larger frontier models and injecting poisoned thoughts.
  • Key claims:
    • Smaller LLMs within the same family can decode reasoning traces of frontier models like GPT-4 or Claude Opus.
    • Extracted reasoning blocks are portable across user sessions and models.
    • Poisoned thoughts can be injected into replayed user conversations to induce unintended model behaviors.
  • Examples:
    • Taking reasoning traces from Opus and injecting them into Kimi or other models.
  • Terminology:
    • cross-model extraction
    • thought poisoning
    • portable encrypted thought
    • autoregression
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates that proprietary model reasoning is not safe from extraction by sophisticated actors using related smaller models.

Security Implications and Mitigations

  • Explanation: Evaluating architectural vulnerabilities, PII/credential leaks in reasoning traces, and potential mitigation strategies for AI labs.
  • Key claims:
    • Reasoning traces frequently leak PII, technical identifiers, and API keys/credentials.
    • Mitigations include context-based envelope defense, stateless verification, and not returning reasoning to users.
    • Architectural revisions are required since simple cryptographic wrapping of reasoning blocks is insufficient.
  • Examples:
    • Leaking API keys and internal IP addresses within model thinking blocks.
  • Terminology:
    • context-based envelope defense
    • pii leakage
    • architectural vulnerability
    • mitigation
  • Why it matters: Highlights severe security and privacy risks when models think out loud and return unencrypted or weakly sealed reasoning traces to end users.

Key Points

Reasoning models think before they answer, but their reasoning is often poorly encrypted.

  • Explanation: Frontier models generate chain-of-thought reasoning tokens before outputting answers, but API wrappers use weak cryptographic seals that can be bypassed.
  • Evidence: Extracted reasoning token counts matched billed API thinking tokens 1:1 across multiple frontier providers.
  • Practical implication: Frontier AI labs cannot rely on simple sealing to protect proprietary reasoning IP or prevent safety leaks.

Reasoning traces are portable across user sessions and model sizes.

  • Explanation: An attacker can extract a reasoning block from a user session on a powerful model and replay it into a smaller or different model.
  • Evidence: Cross-model extraction successfully transferred reasoning traces from large models to smaller models within the same family.
  • Practical implication: Enables advanced prompt injection, model distillation attacks, and behavioral steering at low computational cost.

Reasoning traces leak sensitive data including credentials and PII.

  • Explanation: Because models process raw user inputs during reasoning, they often regurgitate sensitive user data, API keys, and internal state information into the thought block.
  • Evidence: Dataset scans of 350,000 reasoning blocks revealed hundreds of distinct PII items, technical identifiers, and credentials.
  • Practical implication: Exposes enterprises using frontier APIs to massive data privacy violations and security breaches.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Context-Based Envelope Defense

  • How it works: A defense mechanism where reasoning blocks are bound to specific request contexts using authenticated encryption and session identifiers.
  • Components:
    • Session-specific AEAD encryption
    • Stateless verification
    • HMAC integrity checks on reasoning payloads
  • When to use: When serving reasoning-heavy LLMs via APIs to prevent replay and cross-session extraction attacks.

Examples & Case Studies

Researchers extracted hundreds of thousands of reasoning blocks from open GitHub and Hugging Face repositories containing user sessions.

  • Illustrates: The prevalence of accidental reasoning trace leaks by developers testing frontier APIs.
  • Lesson: Users frequently and unknowingly expose proprietary model reasoning data online.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Frontier LLM APIs have severe architectural vulnerabilities in how they handle chain-of-thought reasoning.
    • Reasoning traces frequently contain sensitive credentials and personal identifiable information (PII).
    • Open-source and smaller models can effectively decode and utilize reasoning traces from proprietary frontier models.
  • Strategic:
    • AI labs must adopt robust context-based envelope defenses and stop returning raw reasoning traces to clients.
    • The illusion of security around proprietary chain-of-thought is broken, necessitating fundamental architectural redesigns.
    • Defensive alignment and monitoring must account for cross-model reasoning extraction and thought poisoning.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How can labs effectively monitor model reasoning without exposing vulnerabilities to extraction attacks?
    • What are the long-term governance implications of widespread model reasoning distillation?
    • Can cryptographic sealing of reasoning traces ever be made fully robust against dedicated attackers?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Universal jailbreaks can decode reasoning traces across Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models with 1:1 token matching. (technical)
  • Extracted reasoning blocks frequently contain leaked PII, API keys, and credentials. (empirical)

Notable Quotes

"We found a way to extract hidden reasoning of frontier models using a vulnerability in the APIs of every frontier AI company." (at 0:40) "So recent AI models, they think before they answer." (at 0:42) "You can decode reasoning traces of frontier LLMs of like the most you know advanced ones like GPT's soul using the smaller LLMs within the same family." (at 1:56)

Compressed Summary

  • Frontier LLM APIs leak reasoning traces through weak encryption seals.
  • Cross-model extraction allows smaller models to decode large model thoughts.
  • Reasoning blocks frequently expose sensitive credentials and PII.
  • Robust context-based envelope defenses are required to mitigate model IP theft.
  • Keywords: jailbreak, chain-of-thought, model-extraction, cryptography, llm-security
  • Core insight: Proprietary LLM reasoning traces are vulnerable to universal extraction and decryption attacks, exposing sensitive data and undermining model security.

  - encrypted reasoning
  - jailbreak
  - prompt injection
- **Why it matters**: Exposes how frontier labs rely on weak API sealing mechanisms to hide internal model reasoning, which can be easily circumvented.
### Cross-Model Reasoning Extraction and Thought Poisoning
- **Explanation**: Using smaller open-source models within the same family to extract reasoning traces from larger frontier models and injecting poisoned thoughts.
- **Key claims**:
  - Smaller LLMs within the same family can decode reasoning traces of frontier models like GPT-4 or Claude Opus.
  - Extracted reasoning blocks are portable across user sessions and models.
  - Poisoned thoughts can be injected into replayed user conversations to induce unintended model behaviors.
- **Examples**:
  - Taking reasoning traces from Opus and injecting them into Kimi or other models.
- **Terminology**:
  - cross-model extraction
  - thought poisoning
  - portable encrypted thought
  - autoregression
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates that proprietary model reasoning is not safe from extraction by sophisticated actors using related smaller models.
### Security Implications and Mitigations
- **Explanation**: Evaluating architectural vulnerabilities, PII/credential leaks in reasoning traces, and potential mitigation strategies for AI labs.
- **Key claims**:
  - Reasoning traces frequently leak PII, technical identifiers, and API keys/credentials.
  - Mitigations include context-based envelope defense, stateless verification, and not returning reasoning to users.
  - Architectural revisions are required since simple cryptographic wrapping of reasoning blocks is insufficient.
- **Examples**:
  - Leaking API keys and internal IP addresses within model thinking blocks.
- **Terminology**:
  - context-based envelope defense
  - pii leakage
  - architectural vulnerability
  - mitigation
- **Why it matters**: Highlights severe security and privacy risks when models think out loud and return unencrypted or weakly sealed reasoning traces to end users.
## Key Points
### Reasoning models think before they answer, but their reasoning is often poorly encrypted.
- **Explanation**: Frontier models generate chain-of-thought reasoning tokens before outputting answers, but API wrappers use weak cryptographic seals that can be bypassed.
- **Evidence**: Extracted reasoning token counts matched billed API thinking tokens 1:1 across multiple frontier providers.
- **Practical implication**: Frontier AI labs cannot rely on simple sealing to protect proprietary reasoning IP or prevent safety leaks.
### Reasoning traces are portable across user sessions and model sizes.
- **Explanation**: An attacker can extract a reasoning block from a user session on a powerful model and replay it into a smaller or different model.
- **Evidence**: Cross-model extraction successfully transferred reasoning traces from large models to smaller models within the same family.
- **Practical implication**: Enables advanced prompt injection, model distillation attacks, and behavioral steering at low computational cost.
### Reasoning traces leak sensitive data including credentials and PII.
- **Explanation**: Because models process raw user inputs during reasoning, they often regurgitate sensitive user data, API keys, and internal state information into the thought block.
- **Evidence**: Dataset scans of 350,000 reasoning blocks revealed hundreds of distinct PII items, technical identifiers, and credentials.
- **Practical implication**: Exposes enterprises using frontier APIs to massive data privacy violations and security breaches.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Context-Based Envelope Defense
- **How it works**: A defense mechanism where reasoning blocks are bound to specific request contexts using authenticated encryption and session identifiers.
- **Components**:
  - Session-specific AEAD encryption
  - Stateless verification
  - HMAC integrity checks on reasoning payloads
- **When to use**: When serving reasoning-heavy LLMs via APIs to prevent replay and cross-session extraction attacks.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Researchers extracted hundreds of thousands of reasoning blocks from open GitHub and Hugging Face repositories containing user sessions.
- **Illustrates**: The prevalence of accidental reasoning trace leaks by developers testing frontier APIs.
- **Lesson**: Users frequently and unknowingly expose proprietary model reasoning data online.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Frontier LLM APIs have severe architectural vulnerabilities in how they handle chain-of-thought reasoning.
  - Reasoning traces frequently contain sensitive credentials and personal identifiable information (PII).
  - Open-source and smaller models can effectively decode and utilize reasoning traces from proprietary frontier models.
- **Strategic**:
  - AI labs must adopt robust context-based envelope defenses and stop returning raw reasoning traces to clients.
  - The illusion of security around proprietary chain-of-thought is broken, necessitating fundamental architectural redesigns.
  - Defensive alignment and monitoring must account for cross-model reasoning extraction and thought poisoning.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How can labs effectively monitor model reasoning without exposing vulnerabilities to extraction attacks?
  - What are the long-term governance implications of widespread model reasoning distillation?
  - Can cryptographic sealing of reasoning traces ever be made fully robust against dedicated attackers?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Universal jailbreaks can decode reasoning traces across Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models with 1:1 token matching. (technical)
- Extracted reasoning blocks frequently contain leaked PII, API keys, and credentials. (empirical)
## Notable Quotes
> "We found a way to extract hidden reasoning of frontier models using a vulnerability in the APIs of every frontier AI company." (at 0:40)
> "So recent AI models, they think before they answer." (at 0:42)
> "You can decode reasoning traces of frontier LLMs of like the most you know advanced ones like GPT's soul using the smaller LLMs within the same family." (at 1:56)
## Compressed Summary
- Frontier LLM APIs leak reasoning traces through weak encryption seals.
- Cross-model extraction allows smaller models to decode large model thoughts.
- Reasoning blocks frequently expose sensitive credentials and PII.
- Robust context-based envelope defenses are required to mitigate model IP theft.
- **Keywords**: jailbreak, chain-of-thought, model-extraction, cryptography, llm-security
- **Core insight**: Proprietary LLM reasoning traces are vulnerable to universal extraction and decryption attacks, exposing sensitive data and undermining model security.
